Plaintiff seeks summary judgment that the OPMS kratom products are unreasonably dangerous as a matter of law, for their failure to provide adequate warning or instruction regarding known risks, and for an unreasonably dangerous design. In the alternative, Plaintiff seeks a declaration that OPMS kratom products are “adulterated” and “misbranded” under the Food, Drug and 1

I. INTRODUCTION The facts of this case are unusual in the product liability context, in that the case concerns injuries from a product that it is not approved for human consumption because there is no reasonable basis for the safety of kratom, but kratom has no purpose other than human consumption, and which is nevertheless widely and openly promoted and sold. See Exhibits 1 & 2 (Packages of OPMS discovered at the scene of Harmony Moller’s death); see also, Exhibits 19 & 20 (explaining kratom is not approved for human consumption). Consequently, there are several facts that the Defendants cannot genuinely dispute, as this memorandum will explain. Taken together, these facts yield the unavoidable conclusion that OPMS kratom products are adulterated and misbranded under federal law, have an unreasonably dangerous design and fail to adequately warn users, and specifically failed to adequately warn Harmony Moller. They are therefore unreasonably dangerous, an element of Plaintiff’s claim under the Louisiana Product Liability Act, for which she requests partial summary judgment. Adequacy of warning is a generally a question of fact, Jack v. Alberto-Culver USA, Inc., 949 So. 2d 1256, 1259 (La. 2007); Bloxom v. Bloxom, 512 So. 2d 839, 844 (La. 1987), see also Stapleton v. Kawasaki Heavy Industries, Ltd., 608 F.2d 571, 573 (5th Cir. 1979). However, when the warnings provided by the manufacturer are specific to the circumstances of a claim, the adequacy of the warning oftentimes does not present an issue of fact, and an award of summary judgment is appropriate. Gonsoulin v. Beta USA, Inc., No. CV 24-1005, 2025 WL 2171050, at *11 (E.D. La. July 31, 2025) (citing Broussard v. Procter & Gamble Co., 463 F. Supp. 2d 596, 608-10 2

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 315-1 Filed 03/12/26 Page 3 of 32 (W.D. La. 2006), aff’d, 517 F.3d 767 (5th Cir. 2008)). An issue over whether a product design is unreasonably dangerous is similarly one of fact, typically requiring expert evidence to prove. See Gonsoulin, at *12 (citing Broussard, 463 F. Supp. 2d at 611, and McCarthy v. Danek Med. Inc., 65 F. Supp. 2d 410, 412 (E.D. La. 1999)). As will be seen, the facts of this case do not admit dispute over the inadequate warning and design defects of the OPMS kratom products that killed Harmony Moller. They are unreasonably dangerous as a matter of law. II. Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 315-1 Filed 03/12/26 Page 5 of 32 V. LEGAL STANDARDS / STANDARDS OF REVIEW A. Motions for Partial Summary Judgment “The court shall grant summary judgment if the movant shows that there is no genuine dispute as to any material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 56. Materiality is a matter of substantive law, and “[o]nly disputes over facts that might affect the outcome of the suit under the governing law will properly preclude the entry of summary judgment. Factual disputes that are irrelevant or unnecessary will not be counted.” Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242, 248 (1986). “A fact is considered material when its existence or nonexistence may be essential to plaintiff’s cause of action under the applicable theory of recovery.” Smith v. Our Lady of the Lake Hospital, Inc., 639 So. 2d 730, 751 (La. 1994). “A genuine issue is one about which reasonable persons could disagree.” Hines v. Garrett, 876 So. 2d 764, 765 (La. 2004). In determining whether a genuine issue of material fact exists, the court must view all evidence in the light most favorable to the nonmoving party. Scott v. Harris, 550 U.S. 372, 380 (2007). The party asserting that a material fact “cannot be or is genuinely disputed” must support the assertion by either: (1) citing to particular parts of materials in the record, including depositions, documents, electronically stored information, affidavits or declarations, stipulations (including those made for purposes of the motion only), admissions, interrogatory answers, or other materials; or (2) showing that the materials cited do not establish the absence or presence of a genuine dispute, or that an adverse party cannot produce admissible evidence to support the fact. Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(c)(1)(A)–(B). If the moving party has carried its burden, the non-movant most “come forward with ‘specific facts showing that there is a genuine issue for trial.’” Matsushita Elec. Indus. 5

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 315-1 Filed 03/12/26 Page 6 of 32 Co. v. Zenith Radio Corp., 475 U.S. 574, 587 (1986). The nonmoving party, however, cannot satisfy his summary judgment burden with conclusory allegations, unsubstantiated assertions, or only a scintilla of evidence. Little v. Liquid Air Corp., 37 F.3d 1069, 1075 (5th Cir. 1994) (en banc). “One of the principal purposes of the summary judgment rule is to isolate and dispose of factually unsupported claims or defenses[.]” Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317, 323–24 (1986). If a party bears the burden of proof “to establish the existence of an element essential to that party’s case,” but fails to make a sufficient showing, “Rule 56(c) mandates the entry of summary judgment” against the party. Id. at 322. B. Reasonably Anticipated Use For all LPLA claims, a plaintiff must show that her damages relate to a reasonably anticipated use of the product. Kampen v. American Isuzu Motors, Inc., 157 F.3d 306, 309 (5th Cir. 1998) (en banc); La. R.S. § 9:2800.54(A). The LPLA defines a reasonably anticipated use as “a use or handling of the product that the product's manufacturer should reasonably expect of an ordinary person in the same or similar circumstances.” La. R.S. § 9:2800.53(7). “Reasonably anticipated use” includes those user actions the manufacturer should have reasonably contemplated when designing the product and providing warnings. See Kampen, 157 F.3d at 311. Warning against a specific use does not necessarily relieve the defendant of its duty to design for and adequately warn against the associated risk. Id. at 314. A plaintiff may recover against a defendant who should have known its warning was being disregarded in a particular way. Id., n.6 (citing RPlaintiffment, 3d of Torts, § 2 cmt. l (1998) (Warnings are not a substitute for safe design)). “A manufacturer must anticipate foreseeable misuse and also consider the particular hazard. When a product presents a serious risk of harm, the manufacturer must warn in a manner likely to catch the user's attention.” Krummel v. Bombardier Corp., 206 F.3d 548, 551 (5th Cir. 2000) (citing 6

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 315-1 Filed 03/12/26 Page 7 of 32 Delery v. Prudential Ins. Co. of Am., 643 So.2d 807, 813–814 (La. App. 4th Cir. 1994; quoting Easton v. Chevron Industries, Inc., 602 So.2d 1032 (La. App. 4th Cir. 1992)). C. Inadequate Warning A product is unreasonably dangerous because an adequate warning about the product has not been provided if: (1) at the time the product left its manufacturer's control, the product possessed a characteristic that may cause damage; and (2) the manufacturer failed to use reasonable care to provide an adequate warning of such characteristic and its danger to users and handlers of the product. La. R.S. § 9:2800.57; Gonsoulin v. Beta USA, Inc, 2025 WL 2171050, at *8 (E.D. La. July 31, 2025); Couturier v. Bard Peripheral Vascular, Inc., 548 F. Supp. 3d 596, 609 (E.D. La. 2021). A plaintiff must demonstrate that the product has a potentially damage-causing characteristic and that the manufacturer failed to use reasonable care to provide an adequate warning about this characteristic. Stahl v. Novartis Pharms. Corp., 283 F.3d 254, 264 (5th Cir. 2002). Before reaching the adequacy of the warning, however, a plaintiff must show that the injury arose from a ‘reasonably anticipated use’ of the product. Gonsoulin, 2025 WL 2171050, at *3 (quoting Kelley v. Hanover Ins. Co., 722 So.2d 1133, 1136 (La App. 5th Cir. 1998)). If the trier of fact then determines the inherent danger is not obvious, and the consumer is not aware of or trained to detect it, the adequacy of the warning must be scrutinized. Warren v. Shelter Mutual Ins. Co., 233 So.3d 568, 574 (La. 2017) (quoting Asbestos v. Bordelon, Inc., 726 So. 926, 955 (La. App. 4th Cir. 1998) and Clark v. Jesuit High School of New Orleans, 686 So. 2d 998 (La. App. 4th Cir. 1996).2 Regarding the adequacy of warnings, Louisiana’s pre-LPLA jurisprudence comports with the statute. See Warren, 233 So. 2d at 574. 2 The text of Asbestos and other Louisiana decisions have mistakenly cited to an earlier decision on an unrelated issue in the Clark case, 572, So. 2d 830 (La. App. 4th Cir. 1990). The 1996 citation used in the body of this memorandum cites to the relevant failure to warn decision. 7

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 315-1 Filed 03/12/26 Page 8 of 32 An “adequate warning” contains two components: “the warning must both lead the ordinary user or handler to contemplate the danger in using the product” and “to either use it safely or decline to use it.” Stahl, 283 F.3d 254 at 271 (quoting Thomas C. Galligan, Jr., The Louisiana Products Liability Act: Making Sense of it All, 49 LA. L. REV. 629, 677 (1989)); Couturier 548 F. Supp. 3d at 609 (E.D. La. 2021). An adequate warning “must be: (1) properly worded to signify the intensity of the inherent danger in the product; (2) properly placed on the product so that the consumer cannot avoid seeing it; and (3) it must convey to the consumer that injury or damage can result from a normal or intended use of the product. Id. To determine if a warning is adequate, Louisiana law considers the severity of the danger, the likelihood that the warning will catch the attention of those who may foreseeably encounter the risk, the intensity and form of the warning, and the cost of improving the strength or mode of the warning. Gonsoulin, 2025 WL 2171050 at *11 (citing Bloxom v. Bloxom, 512 So.2d 839, 844 (La. 1987); Asbestos, 726 So. 2d at 956 (citing Clark 686 So. 2d at 1002). D. Unreasonably Dangerous Design Under the LPLA, a product's design is unreasonably dangerous if the plaintiff demonstrates that, at the time the product left the manufacturer's control, “[t]here existed an alternative design for the product that was capable of preventing the claimant's damage and that the danger of the damage outweighed the burden on the manufacturer of adopting the alternative design.” Fuller v. Eisai Inc., 513 F. Supp.3d 710, 717-18 (E.D. La. 2021); Guidry v. Janssen Pharms., Inc., 206 F. Supp. 3d 1187, 1198 (E.D. La. 2016); La. R.S. 9:2800.56. To determine whether an alternative design was capable of preventing the damage, Louisiana courts apply a cause-in-fact analysis that can use either or both “but for” and substantial factors tests. Couturier, 548 F. Supp. 3d at 608 (citing Quick v. Murphy Oil Co., 643 So. 2d 1291, 1295 (La. Ct. App. 1994) and Thomas v. 8

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 315-1 Filed 03/12/26 Page 9 of 32 Missouri Pacific R.R. Co., 466 So. 2d 1280, 1285 (La. 1985)). An alternative design need only reduce the likelihood or extent of damages, not completely prevent them. Gonsoulin, at *13; see also Bernard, 689 So. 2d at 560. To conduct the risk-utility analysis, courts begin with determining what risk the product created, including the effect of a warning, if it was adequate. Couturier, 548 F. Supp. 3d at 608 (citing Bernard v. Ferrellgas, Inc., 689 So. 2d 554, 560 (La. Ct. App. 1997)). They then ask if a reasonable person would conclude that the danger-in-fact, whether foreseeable or not, outweighs the utility of the product. Couturier, 548 F. Supp. 3d at 608; Bernard, 689 So. 2d at 561. VI. ARGUMENT A. Because Human Consumption was a Reasonably Anticipated Use Regardless of Defendants’ Disclaimers, the Defendants had a Duty to Design Against, and to Warn Harmony Moller of, the Risk of Death from Ingestion of OPMS Kratom. The Plaintiff has provided evidence demonstrating how kratom products, and their characteristic alkaloids including mitragynine, 7-Hydroxymitragynine (7-OH), and mitragynine pseudo indoxyl cause addiction, toxicity, and death in humans, infra at VI.B.1. In brief, kratom usage, especially when prolonged, can lead to addiction; to kratom toxicity, affecting multiple organs; and to cardiorespiratory arrest. See e.g. Exhibits 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 29, 30, 38, 53, & 54. The Plaintiff has also shown through competent evidence that OPMS kratom is knowingly sold with an expectation that buyers will ingest the product. It is not only foreseeable that users will ingest OPMS kratom, but the Defendants also expect the product to be used this way, and they market it for uses that require human consumption. See Exhibit 9 at 97:19-22; Exhibit 8 at 37:2- 12; and Exhibit 32 (JOpen, LLC’s Responses and Objections to Plaintiff’s Requests for Admission at No. 9 (“Request For Admission No. 9: Admit that JOPEN Marketed and sold kratom products for human consumption. Response: Admit.”). In fact, Defendants intend for OPMS kratom to be 9

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 315-1 Filed 03/12/26 Page 10 of 32 ingested for the unapproved medicinal purpose of assisting in the treatment of opiate use disorder. Exhibit 14 at 65:15-66:15; Exhibit 5 159:18-23 and pp.160:19-161:2; and Exhibit 4 at 206:23- 207:10. The self-serving disavowals on the Defendants’ packaging, are not evidence of the contrary; rather, they illustrate the deceptive nature of the Defendants’ business, conduct, and marketing practices. Exhibits 1 & 2 (Claiming OPMS Silver kratom is a “botanical specimen”). Defendants have offered no evidence that the purported benefits and purposes of OPMS kratom products could be achieved without human consumption. The Defendants’ description of OPMS kratom as a “botanical specimen” does not relieve them of their duties to safely design products, adequately warn against dangers and to avoid marketing adulterated and misbranded products. A “botanical specimen” intended for scientific, or research purposes would consist of a whole or partial sample of an actual plant, not a processed powder.3 Neither do scientists primarily obtain them in smoke shops, convenience stores, or health food stores. The noun “botanical,” however, refers to “a drug made from part of a plant, as from roots, leaves, bark or berries.” Collins English Dictionary, 2019. It is clear that Defendants are selling the latter “botanical specimen,” and not the former. For instance, Martian Sales agrees that a botanical specimen is “just a specimen of a botanical, like a piece of a leaf.” Exhibit 9 (Excerpt of October 8, 2025, 30(b)(6) Deposition of Mark Reilly Corporate Representative of Martian Sales) at 97:1-4; see also, Exhibit 10 (Excerpt of October 9, 2025 30(b)(6) Deposition of Mark Jennings Corporate Representative of LP IND, LLC) at 35:17-21 (Stating “It’s a plant or part of a plant.”). Response: Admit.”). “A warning against product misuse is relevant to assessing what uses of its product a manufacturer reasonably anticipates.” Kampen, 157 F.3d at 314. The en banc U.S. Fifth Circuit discussed a hypothetical in Kampen that is on all fours with the case at bar: Our holding will not…allow malevolent manufacturers to absolve themselves from liability for uses (or misuses) of their products which the evidence shows should have been reasonably anticipated despite a warning to the contrary…. It would be legally ineffective if, for example, Isuzu had warned against using its jack to change the tires on the Impulse, a user had nonetheless used the jack to change a tire and was injured in the process. In that case, a court should find that, despite the 11

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 315-1 Filed 03/12/26 Page 12 of 32 warning, using a factory-supplied jack to change a tire (which is the very purpose for which the jack was supplied) is …unquestionably a reasonably anticipated use. Id., n.5. Defendants “warn” users that OPMS Silver is a “only for use as a botanical specimen,” and “cannot advise on its use” but intend that the product be ingested. Exhibits 1 & 2; see also, Exhibits 8, 9, and 32. This is exactly the same as a car manufacturer telling a purchaser not to use its jack to change a tire. As the Fifth Circuit instructs, this Court must find that ingestion is unquestionably a reasonably anticipated use of OPMS kratom products, and that Defendants’ “warning” is legally ineffective. Because ingestion was a reasonably anticipated use of Defendants’ manufacture, distribution and sale of OPMS kratom products, and because ingestion may cause illness and death, the Court must analyze the Plaintiff’s failure to warn and design defects claims and evidence on their merits. B. Defendants’ failure to adequately warn Harmony Moller and other kratom users of their risk of sudden death or instruct them on preventing it renders OPMS kratom products unreasonably dangerous under the LPLA. 1. OPMS kratom products contained the damaging and deadly ingredients mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine upon leaving the Defendants’ control. Defendants do not contest the presence of mitragynine and 7-OH in their product; on the rear of the package, in small print, they list the mass and content of percentage comprised of the deadly ingredients. Exhibits 1 & 2. Yet they fail to list the numerous other pharmacologically active alkaloids identified in product testing. See e.g., Exhibits 41-50 (product testing documents listing additional alkaloids present in the product at issue such as such as payantheine, speciogynine, speciociliatine, mitraphylline, and isoryhncophylline). The damaging characteristic of all identified and unidentified alkaloids was known to the manufacturer to be present, when the product left the manufacturers control. 12

More importantly, they cannot marshal admissible evidence that raises a question of material fact concerning the dangers of kratom use, while the Plaintiff, Kathleen Moller, has presented overwhelming evidence of the dangers posed by these kratom alkaloids. Defendants rely on two extremely limited and narrow clinical studies, one profoundly biased as it is funded by Defendants themselves, for the proposition that kratom is safe. Yet their own experts acknowledge the studies are of insufficient power to render generalizable opinions to all kratom users and are not applicable to Harmony Moller specifically. See Exhibit 27 at 82:23-83:10 (Dr. Christopher McCurdy confirming that the Mitra-leaf study funded by Johnson Foods cannot be generalized to individuals with underlying cardiac conditions and polypharmacy); and 101:11-18 (Stating that none of the clinical studies relied on by Defendants are “of sufficient power to thoroughly characterize the safety profile of kratom…”); see also Exhibit 26 at 23:22-24 (Confirming Dr. Huestis’ clinical study of kratom was funded by ). Indeed, the FDA has been reporting of dangers associated to Kratom since at least August 18, 2015, when it issued an import alert stating in part: “In fact, the scientific literature disclosed serious concerns regarding the toxicity of kratom in multiple organ systems. Consumption of kratom can lead to a number of health impacts, including respiratory depression, nervousness, agitation, aggression, sleeplessness, hallucinations, delusions, tremors, loss of libido, constipation, skin hyperpigmentation, nausea, vomiting, and severe withdrawal signs and symptoms.” Exhibit 18 (FDA Import alert listing for human and animal drugs, indicating Import Alter 54-15 was published on August 18, 2015, accessible at: https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/cms_ia/industry_66.html?utm_source%201/6, last accessed 13

The dangers inherent in using OPMS kratom products are not obvious to its users. OPMS kratom products appear to be a powder prepared for ingestion as a capsule or mixed in with a beverage. Exhibits 1 & 2. Because the sale of food, supplements, drugs and medicines is highly regulated, see FDCA, 21 U.S.C. § 301 et seq., consumers encountering such products on the open market, in a store, do not have reason to consider them deadly. The dangerous kratom alkaloids, being an intrinsic, invisible component that is not detectable without chemical analysis, are inherently not obvious to a user. See Exhibits 41-50 (Product testing documents showing product contents and potency not listed on product labels (Exhibits 1 & 2)). Because OPMS kratom presents no obvious danger to a prospective consumer, the Defendants are required to provide an adequate warning of its dangerous content. Warren, 233 So.3d at 574; Hooker v. Super Products Corp., 751 So.2d 889, 905 (La. App. 5th Cir. 1999); Asbestos, 726 So. at 955. 3. Defendants failed as a matter of law to use reasonable care to provide an adequate warning of the dangers of using OPMS kratom products, including the risk of death. or to instruct users how to avoid addiction, toxicity, or death when using the product. a. Defendants’ warning was inadequate as to the risks of using their product. The U.S. Fifth Circuit has noted that “a mere reference to an adverse effect is not necessarily an ‘adequate warning’ under the LPLA. The warning must contain language that is adequate to reasonably inform the recipient … about the nature of the danger involved.” Stahl, 14

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 315-1 Filed 03/12/26 Page 15 of 32 283 F.3d at 267. In the case at bar, the package warning does not even contain a single mention of the possibility of death, the ultimate “adverse effect.” See Exhibits 1 & 2. This alone is sufficient to render the Defendants’ warning inadequate to the risks run by their products’ users. Nor does it contain a mention of the possibility of addiction, let alone how addiction increases the chance of overdose and death. Id., see also, Exhibits 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 29, and 30. The Plaintiff has proffered expert evidence as to the warning’s inadequacies. This evidence shows that the warning was insufficient under every factor Louisiana law considers. The record indicates the warning did not adequately present the severity of the danger. See generally, Exhibit 39 (Expert Report of Sarah Kowitt, Ph.D.). As already noted, the mention of death and addiction alone would not suffice to reasonably inform a prospective user of the danger. The warning requirement seeks to “lead the ordinary user or handler to contemplate the danger in using the product.” Couturier, 548 F. Supp. 3d at 609 (emphasis added). In addition to the severity of the consequences, the placement, intensity and form of the warning provided are wholly inadequate to the risk of sudden death in the course of normal use. When a risk is deadly, the LPLA requires more than a laundry list of potential adverse effects in small print, which may not be read until after consuming the product. Rather, the size, location and prominence of the warning must be commensurate with the nature of the risk. Indeed, given Defendants easily changed labeling in the past, it should be easy to update the package warning label with changes such as clearly communicating the health risks associated to kratom (like cardiac adverse effects and risk of death), communicating how to minimize risks through clear guidance on dosage and timeframes for use, and by complying by warning best practices, such as use of clear familiar words, prominent placement of the warning, or use of icons or symbols to increase attention. See generally, Exhibit 39 (Expert Report of Sarah Kowitt, Ph.D.); see also, 15

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 315-1 Filed 03/12/26 Page 16 of 32 Exhibit 5 at 67:1-17; 68:22-24 (discussing updating product labels to list the false distributor entity, Choice Organics). “Numerous decisions confirm that the physical characteristics of the warning itself are pertinent to … adequacy. The warning's conspicuousness, prominence, and size of print, in comparison to the print size employed for other parts of the manufacturer's message, must be adequate to alert the reasonably prudent person.” Gonsoulin, at 10 (quoting Madden, Owen & Davis, Madden & Owen on Products Liability § 9:10).
